title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Ypsilanti hits pause on electrical upgrades tied to a big U-M data center plan.

lines.text: Good evening and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're digging into Ypsilanti Township's decision this week to pause major electrical projects while they study a proposed University of Michigan research computing center.
That moratorium on high-voltage facilities is the big story tonight, Graham. Let's start there.
Exactly. The township board approved a 180-day pause on new or expanded high-voltage utility facilities. It's aimed at studying impacts from that U-M project backed by Los Alamos National Laboratory.
Why now? What's driving this pause specifically in Washtenaw County?
Residents and officials are worried about the power demands. The project would add significant load to a regional grid already strained by AI growth across the state.
And how does this fit into the bigger picture we've seen with other townships?
It's part of a growing wave. Garfield Township just voted yesterday to halt all new data center proposals for a year to study power, water and noise limits.
That gives residents breathing room before any rules change, right?
Precisely. Without the pause, developers could file applications before new restrictions kick in. Lowell Township is still hammering out its own ordinance after months of debate.
What about the electric bill angle? How do these projects affect ratepayers?
That's the core concern. Taxpayers within driving distance often end up paying for utility upgrades needed to support these big loads.
We've also heard about the Campbell coal plant staying open to feed data center demand. How does that connect?

The U.S. Department of Energy ordered the J.H. Campbell plant in Ottawa County to keep running last Monday, citing rising electricity needs from data centers. It means continued emissions and higher costs for western Michigan ratepayers.
So the energy picture is shifting fast because of AI growth. What about water use?
A new state proposal would force operators to disclose how much water their facilities consume. Michigan residents near proposed sites are worried about strain on aquifers and municipal supplies.
That disclosure bill aims to give communities data before approvals, correct?
Yes. It's one of several measures lawmakers are reviewing this week, including changes to taxes and power rules that could speed up or slow projects needing hundreds of megawatts.
Township supervisors across northern Michigan endorsed rules today that would force data centers to pay more toward grid upgrades. How might that help residents?
If those bills pass, locals could see lower electric bills, but only if local governments keep leverage over the big projects. It signals real pushback against unlimited growth.
St. Joseph County is also drafting noise rules for 24/7 facilities. What are residents there most concerned about?
The constant hum and potential higher electric rates if big loads come online. Officials are tracking extra power pull from the regional grid too.
Wixom may lift its data center freeze months early. What could that mean for Oakland County suburbs?
It would reopen the door for proposals that have already sparked pushback. Residents could soon face decisions on large power-hungry projects affecting local rates and land use.
Back to Ypsilanti — what happens during this 180-day study period?
The board wants to examine impacts on the grid, water and the community from that specific U-M research center proposal. It buys time to weigh jobs and tax revenue against the demands.
Washtenaw leaders are pitching the project as an economic win. How are they framing the benefits?
They're highlighting jobs and tax revenue while residents question the power and water demands. The outcome will shape future development in the county.
This feels like a pattern across the state. How many places have taken similar pauses?
Several townships are moving in that direction this week alone. Garfield, Lowell and now Ypsilanti are all reviewing limits on power, noise and siting.
What role does the University of Michigan play here with the Los Alamos connection?
It's a research computing center proposal. The backing from Los Alamos National Laboratory adds a layer of federal interest, but the local grid impacts are what the township is studying first.
How might this moratorium affect the timeline for any potential project?
It delays new or expanded high-voltage facilities for six months. That gives everyone time to gather data on costs and benefits before decisions are locked in.
And for folks 30 or 60 miles away, why should they care about what happens in Ypsilanti?
Because grid upgrades and rate impacts often ripple across the region. What one township decides can set precedents for neighboring counties facing similar proposals.
We've seen Lansing weighing tax breaks and power rules. Any sense of how these local pauses might influence state action?
Local pushback is feeding into the broader legislative debate. Bills on disclosure, cost sharing and siting are all moving this week.
What happens next if the study finds significant risks?
The township could adopt stricter rules on where facilities locate and what limits apply to power and noise, similar to what's underway in Lowell.
And if the data looks manageable?
Projects could move forward with conditions. Either way, the pause ensures the community has a say before anything is built.
This ties into farmland and town character too. How are those factors playing in?
Large server farms can affect roads, taxes and the overall feel of rural areas. Garfield supervisors specifically called out impacts on local taxes, roads and the power grid in Grand Traverse County.
So it's not just electricity — it's the full local footprint.
Right. Water draw, noise and land use all factor into these debates.
Let's shift to quick hits. Graham, what's the latest on Garfield Township's year-long halt?
Supervisors voted yesterday to pause all new proposals while they research limits. It prevents developers from filing before rules are set.
Lowell Township is still working on its ordinance after months of debate. What will those rules cover?
Where facilities can locate and limits on power and noise. Kent County residents are watching closely for tax and development impacts.
The water disclosure bill is another one from this week. Why is that important for communities?
It requires operators to report consumption. That data helps residents near sites assess strain on aquifers before approvals.
Lansing is reviewing multiple bills on taxes and electricity. What could change for projects needing hundreds of megawatts?
The proposals could either speed things up or add hurdles, affecting how quickly these big loads come online statewide.
St. Joseph County is drafting noise rules. Any details on the 24/7 concern?
Officials are also tracking grid pull. Residents within 30 miles worry about constant hum and higher rates.
Wixom may end its moratorium early. What's the potential impact there?
It could reopen the door for proposals in Oakland County suburbs that have already drawn pushback over rates and land use.
And the Campbell plant decision from Monday — how is that reshaping the energy picture?
Keeping the aging coal unit online means continued emissions and costs for western Michigan ratepayers amid rising data center demand.
Now for on deck. What's coming up that listeners can attend?
Solon Township Planning Commission met yesterday on zoning ordinance revisions for data centers, including special land use provisions.
That one wrapped up, but it shows the ongoing local work on these rules.
Exactly. Check the Michigan Data Center Tracker for the latest agendas and any new meetings popping up.
Listeners should stay tuned — these local decisions are shaping the state's data center future.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Ypsilanti Township Pauses Power Projects Over Data Center Concerns
